top.title: Razorback Report Card: Auburn Postgame
top.description: Nov 7, 2026; Auburn, Alabama, USA; Arkansas Razorbacks running back Cam Settles (27) carries against the Auburn Tigers during the first quarter at Jordan-Hare Stadium. Mandatory Credit: John Reed-Imagn Images | Source: Lastwordonsports.com - Kate Pearson Halyburton, Editor The Razorbacks had the lead, explosive runs, and a late answer on offense. They still could not contain Byrum Brown or finish a game they had every opportunity to win. Arkansas does not need a participation trophy for making a loss more competitive. The Razorbacks needed a victory. They built an early lead, carried an advantage into the fourth quarter, and delivered a late touchdown to tie the game. Then Auburn drove into field-goal range and won 26-23 on Alex McPherson’s 43-yard kick with 33 seconds remaining. Razorback Report Card: Auburn Postgame Arkansas fell to 3-6 overall and 1-5 in SEC play. Yes, this was better than Missouri. That is a remarkably low bar for a program asking supporters to remain invested in its direction. The pregame report card established the expectations before kickoff. Contain Brown. Establish the running game. Protect possessions. Finish opportunities. Those standards do not become unreasonable because Arkansas failed to meet them. Run Defense: F The assignment was not a secret. Keep Brown from becoming Auburn’s most dependable rushing threat. Maintain responsibilities when he leaves the pocket. Make the Tigers find another answer. The pregame benchmark required Arkansas to hold Brown below 60 rushing yards and prevent a quarterback run of 20 yards or more. He finished with 120 yards, including a 39-yard fourth-quarter run. That is not narrowly missing the target. That lets the specific problem identified before kickoff become a central reason for losing. Brown gained 125 rushing yards after halftime, overcoming his negative first-half total. His five-yard touchdown run gave Auburn its first lead. His later rushing contributions helped the Tigers produce their final touchdown and winning field-goal drive. Arkansas deserves credit for containing him early. It can’t hide behind that first half after he took control of the second. A defensive plan is not successful simply because it worked before the opponent adjusted. Responding to that adjustment is part of the job. Pass Defense: D The passing yardage was manageable. The moments were not. Brown threw two touchdown passes after halftime and completed 10 of 14 second-half attempts. Arkansas disrupted him early, then allowed him to become more efficient when Auburn needed production most. The defining failure came on third-and-12 in the fourth quarter. Arkansas had an opportunity to sack Brown. Instead, he escaped and found Keshaun Singleton for a 28-yard touchdown that put Auburn ahead 23-16 with 3:56 remaining. top.title: UCF football gets late heroics from Alonza Barnett III in wild win over Kansas
top.description: UCF threw away a three-score, second-half lead on the road for the second time in just over a month. Only this time, Alonza Barnett III — the redshirt senior brought in from James Madison to lead the Knights back to prominence — delivered a signature, final-minute drive for the win. Barnett hit tight end Caden Piening for a 6-yard touchdown pass with one second remaining, and Will Stone knocked through the decisive PAT in a 33-32 rally past Kansas on Nov. 7 at David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium. The Knights improved to 5-4 overall and 3-3 in the Big 12, moving to within one win of bowl eligibility with three games left. More importantly, Scott Frost and his players finally silenced the conversation of UCF's woes on the road. The 12-game skid, dating back to September 2024, is dead. Asked if he could describe his emotions after watching the Knights surrender a 26-7 lead and complete a final comeback, Frost said, "I could try to describe it, but it would come up short." "We've been involved in two pretty special games, as good of college football games as I've been involved (with) in a long time," Frost added, referring to UCF's double-overtime win over BYU on Oct. 24. "I thought it was two evenly matched teams and just the way the game went was really strange to me. I feel blessed that we were able to go down and get the play at the end of the game." Here are three takeaways from another dramatic Big 12 battle. Alonza Barnett III rewards UCF's faith with clutch drive Saturday's final drive was exactly what Frost and his staff envisioned when pursuing Barnett in the transfer portal, and exactly what Knights fans hoped to see in an experienced, accomplished quarterback. Barnett suffered a hamstring injury on the final drive of UCF's 12-7 loss at Pittsburgh on Sept. 12. He missed the next five games, only returning to action in a backup role last week in a blowout defeat to Baylor . Concerns for Barnett's mobility were put to rest in the first half as he scrambled away from pressure and picked up several nice gains on designed run plays. And he provided an element in the vertical passing game that was noticeably absent for two months, connecting on a 44-yard strike to Josh Derry that gave UCF a 26-7 lead little more than five minutes into the second half. "I (saw) a dawg, somebody that was hungry to come out there and prove himself, especially missing so many games," Derry said. Kansas stymied UCF on three straight drives as the defensive line trio of Blake Herold, Leroy Harris III and David Santiago imposed its will. They were responsible for 9½ of the Jayhawks' 11 tackles for loss on the day, including Harris' three sacks. That coincided with Kansas catching fire and scoring 25 unanswered points, reclaiming the lead with 1:06 to play on Dylan Edwards' 2-yard hurdle into the end zone. top.title: U17WWC: You’ve written your names in gold – Tinubu tells Flamingos
top.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru President Bola Tinubu has congratulated Nigeria’s Flamingos for making history as the first African team to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup following their 2-1 victory over Japan in Saturday’s final in Rabat, Morocco. The president, who received the cheering news upon his return from campaign engagements in Akwa Ibom and Rivers States, hailed Nigeria’s maiden triumph as a proud moment for the nation and a landmark achievement for African women’s football. “What wonderful news to return home to! Our young girls have conquered the world and given Nigerians everywhere another reason to celebrate our great country. “To our gallant Flamingos, I say congratulations. You have shown courage, discipline, determination, and the Nigerian spirit of never giving up. “I followed your journey throughout this tournament, and after your semi-final victory, you promised to bring the trophy home. Today, you have kept that promise. You believed in yourselves, fought for one another, and carried our nation’s flag to the very top of the world. “Your victory is an inspiration to millions of young Nigerian girls who dream of achieving greatness. You have shown them that with hard work, opportunity, and determination, they too can reach the highest levels of achievement. “Today, Nigeria celebrates you. You have written your names in gold, and your country is immensely proud of you.” The president particularly applauds Awawu Bashiru and Oluebube Umejiaku, whose goals secured the historic victory, while commending the entire squad for their exceptional teamwork throughout the tournament. He also congratulates the coaching crew, the Nigeria Football Federation, and the National Sports Commission for their contributions to the team’s success. President Tinubu reaffirms his administration’s commitment to investing in grassroots sports development and expanding opportunities for young Nigerians, particularly girls, to discover, nurture, and fulfill their potential. “Congratulations once again, Flamingos. Thank you for making Nigeria proud.” The post U17WWC: You’ve written your names in gold – Tinubu tells Flamingos appeared first on Vanguard News .

top.title: One daring shot was all La Salle needed to repeat as state soccer champs
top.description: PROVIDENCE – Camryn Bromage just couldn't help herself, and that turned out to be the best thing for La Salle on this Saturday afternoon at Rhode Island College. The junior midfielder had time to take a shot midway through the first half against Cumberland. That it was from all of 35 yards, or that coach Stephanie Goulet would have preferred a pass elsewhere, will ultimately just become details in a story they'll remember for years to come. Bromage managed to find the net and make the difference at Alumni Stadium as the Rams sealed back-to-back Division I titles with a 1-0 win over the Clippers under gray skies on Nov. 7. "My coach was like, 'Do not take that shot.' It was a little far out," Bromage said. "But I had the space, I had the opportunity and I just shot it." Watch RI high school sports on NFHS! Bromage took aim in the 15th minute after a tense start between a pair of familiar contenders. Her right-footed effort skipped at the top of the 6-yard box and found its way inside the right post, aided by turf still slick from the overnight rain. That moment allowed La Salle to flip what was its lone defeat of the season, a loss by the same score line against Cumberland at home. "It's a wet game," Bromage said. "The field is slippery. It just so happened it went through." The Rams kept a 12th clean sheet of the season to bring this one home, with central defender Jill Handrahan claiming tournament Most Valuable Player honors. Grace Keenan was forced to make just two saves, and one of those came off a corner kick when Shea Maher tried to force one home with her chest in the 54th minute. "I know a lot of the girls on their team," Handrahan said. "I know how good they are. Going into it I was a little nervous." The Clippers nearly opened the scoring in the first minute. Paynter Maher's cross off the right wing flashed across an open net, but Milana Izzo couldn't get a touch on it to put it away. Cumberland didn't force a save from Keenan before the break, with La Salle gradually taking control of the play as the half progressed. "I feel like we brought the energy," Handrahan said. "Everybody was just working so hard." The Rams (14-1-3) and Clippers (15-2-2) exploded for a combined 12 goals while dispatching North Kingstown and Mt. Hope, respectively, in the semifinals. This was a different sort of 80 minutes in the title round, and La Salle joined the Skippers among programs to finish off recent repeat titles at the top level. North Kingstown beat the Rams in 2021 and 2022 before La Salle returned the favor in 2025. "It's hard to win it two times in a row," Bromage said. "I'm just so happy we were able to accomplish that for our seniors and for everybody." CUMBERLAND (0): No scoring. LA SALLE (1): Camryn Bromage; assist – Lila Slagle. Halftime – LS, 1-0. top.title: Norfolk State’s Michael Vick gives explanation for failed victory formation in 29-28 loss
top.description: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images Norfolk State’s Michael Vick gives explanation for failed victory formation in 29-28 loss appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . It looked like Michael Vick and his Norfolk State Spartans were closing in on a huge in-conference win against a surging North Carolina Central Eagles team , but the unthinkable happened with 1:34 left. North Carolina Central had no timeouts, and Norfolk State had the ball and could have run out the clock to secure the victory. But instead, the Spartans ran another play and ultimately fumbled, leading North Carolina Central to recover and ultimately score a touchdown to surge ahead 29-28. Michael Vick on the crucial fumble that opened the door for Norfolk State's stunning defeat to North Carolina Central. @WTKR3 pic.twitter.com/rJBWUCF9Dx — Marc Davis (@marcdavissports) November 7, 2026 Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) In postgame comments, Vick tried to explain what happened. “I don’t know what happened at the end of the game. I put my headset down, I called victory formation. All we had to do was just take a knee and nail the clock out. That’s just situational football. I don’t know what happened in regards to that. I looked up and we was running the ball, and then I seen the fumble. But my final instructions was victory formation. That’s when you kneel it out, and they had, I think, zero timeouts left, and the game was over practically.” When a reporter asked him to clarify, Vick repeated that he called victory and said he doesn’t know why a run play was called. “I put my headset down, and I took my headset off ’cause all we had to do was just run it three times, or two times, or kneel it out. I just called victory. I don’t know what happened. A run play was called. I looked up, I seen us running the ball. I don’t know what happened. I really don’t. I don’t know what the play call was. I don’t know why we even ran that play.” Vick said the play will be used as a teaching example across the country and stressed once more that he called victory formation. “People will look at that and that’ll go on as a teaching tape for a lot of teams across the country for years to come. I hate it had to be us, but I called victory formation. I’m just letting everybody know that.” Related: North Carolina Central narrowly beat Michael Vick, Norfolk State 29-28 Related: The anatomy of an upset: Fort Valley State beats Florida A&M in early season action

And that scene could very well spark the final days of the junior Buckeyes wideout, per Damien Harris. The former New England Patriots running back turned CBS Sports analyst weighed in on Smith’s Columbus future. And Harris’s words will turn heads and grab eyeballs. “He’s done, he’s going to pack it up. In my opinion, there’s nothing to gain, there’s everything to lose if you’re Jeremiah Smith. I don’t think that he plays again the rest of the season for Ohio State,” Harris proclaimed. “What’s there to play for? This isn’t a College Football Playoff team. That could very well be Smith’s last game inside the Horseshoe amid his NFL Draft chatter. Smith continues to garner top pick hype especially before facing the Ducks. Hence why Harris believes it’s time to shut down Smith if you’re Day and OSU. top.description: Sophie Cunningham ©Credits: IMAGO “In the women’s game, is it really about how good you are or the visibility, how pretty you are?” Angel McCoughtry has set off a big debate with this one question. The five-time WNBA All-Star said on the Get to the Point podcast that looks and visibility can matter more than talent when it comes to endorsements, and she used Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham as her example. When the hosts asked if she thought Caitlin Clark was pretty, McCoughtry laughed and moved on without answering. The clip drew a fast response from analysts on Fox News’ The Big Weekend Show , and one host said what bothered her most. “It’s amazing to me how the WNBA and the players in the WNBA, their league is getting attention that helps and benefits all of them, but you see certain players actively badmouthing the ones who are bringing the attention, the money, and the eyeballs to their league. nigeria.title: U17WWC: You’ve written your names in gold – Tinubu tells Flamingos
nigeria.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru President Bola Tinubu has congratulated Nigeria’s Flamingos for making history as the first African team to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup following their 2-1 victory over Japan in Saturday’s final in Rabat, Morocco. The president, who received the cheering news upon his return from campaign engagements in Akwa Ibom and Rivers States, hailed Nigeria’s maiden triumph as a proud moment for the nation and a landmark achievement for African women’s football. “What wonderful news to return home to! Our young girls have conquered the world and given Nigerians everywhere another reason to celebrate our great country. “To our gallant Flamingos, I say congratulations. You have shown courage, discipline, determination, and the Nigerian spirit of never giving up. “I followed your journey throughout this tournament, and after your semi-final victory, you promised to bring the trophy home. Today, you have kept that promise. You believed in yourselves, fought for one another, and carried our nation’s flag to the very top of the world. “Your victory is an inspiration to millions of young Nigerian girls who dream of achieving greatness. You have shown them that with hard work, opportunity, and determination, they too can reach the highest levels of achievement. “Today, Nigeria celebrates you. You have written your names in gold, and your country is immensely proud of you.” The president particularly applauds Awawu Bashiru and Oluebube Umejiaku, whose goals secured the historic victory, while commending the entire squad for their exceptional teamwork throughout the tournament. He also congratulates the coaching crew, the Nigeria Football Federation, and the National Sports Commission for their contributions to the team’s success. President Tinubu reaffirms his administration’s commitment to investing in grassroots sports development and expanding opportunities for young Nigerians, particularly girls, to discover, nurture, and fulfill their potential. “Congratulations once again, Flamingos. Thank you for making Nigeria proud.” The post U17WWC: You’ve written your names in gold – Tinubu tells Flamingos appeared first on Vanguard News .

nigeria.title: AMERICA IS NOT NIGERIA: Why Trump’s midterm defeat cannot predict Tinubu’s 2027 fortunes
nigeria.description: By Kayode Akinmade The sweeping defeat suffered by President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the November 3 American midterm elections has predictably provided fresh ammunition for Nigeria’s opposition politicians, who are already attempting to draw parallels between the political fortunes of the American president and those of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections. While the comparison may offer an attractive political talking point, it is, at best, superficial and, at worst, a deliberate attempt to transplant the political circumstances of one country into another. There is no doubt that the Republican defeat represents a significant setback for Trump. Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a powerful electoral rebuke to the Republican administration and signalling widespread dissatisfaction with some of its policies. The result has opened a new chapter in American politics and raised questions about the direction of Trump’s presidency. However, the critical question is whether the circumstances that produced this outcome in the United States are sufficiently comparable to Nigeria’s political and economic realities to justify the conclusion that Tinubu is destined for a similar electoral fate in 2027. The conflict, which has lasted several months, has heightened concerns about American military involvement abroad, increased pressure on energy markets and contributed to rising fuel prices. For American households already grappling with the cost of living, the war became another source of economic anxiety. Its financial implications, military casualties and uncertain strategic objectives also generated questions about the wisdom of the administration’s foreign policy choices. nigeria.title: Countdown to 2027: Edo North is for Oshiomhole

Oshiomhole has moved from delivering roads to delivering accountability, and Edo North have seen the difference in both bricks and budgets. nigeria.title: A Ballot on a Burial Date? Northern Nigeria Confronts the Symbolism of January 16
nigeria.description: By Hassan A Karofi The choice of dates in politics is often presented as a matter of administrative convenience. Yet history teaches us that dates carry powerful symbolism, especially in societies where collective memories of tragedy and triumph remain deeply rooted. As Nigeria prepares for a presidential election scheduled for January 16, 2026, it is important to reflect on what that date means to millions of people, particularly in Northern Nigeria, where January 16 is associated with one of the darkest episodes in the country’s history. The significance of January 16 cannot be understood without revisiting the events of the country’s first military coup. In the early hours of January 15, 1966, a group of young military officers launched Nigeria’s first coup d’état. By the morning of January 16, the consequences of the coup were evident. Several of Nigeria’s most prominent political and military leaders had been assassinated. Among those killed were Sir Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto and Premier of Northern Nigeria; Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, Nigeria’s first Prime Minister; Brigadier Samuel Ademulegun; Brigadier Zakariya Maimalari; and other senior political and military figures. While leaders from different regions were affected, the perception in the North was that the coup disproportionately targeted Northern political leadership. This perception would profoundly shape political attitudes and inter-ethnic relations for decades. The events following the coup further deepened Northern grievances. Major General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi assumed power and suspended parts of the constitutional order. In many parts of Northern Nigeria, suspicion and anger grew rapidly, culminating in the counter-coup of July 1966. The resulting instability ultimately contributed to the chain of events that led to the Nigerian Civil War. More than six decades later, the memory of January 1966 remains alive. For many Northern families, historians, traditional institutions, and political observers, January 16 is not merely another date on the calendar. It is a reminder of a traumatic turning point that altered Nigeria’s political trajectory and claimed the lives of leaders who continue to be revered across the region. Against this backdrop, the decision to hold a presidential election on January 16 raises legitimate questions. Whether the date was chosen for logistical, constitutional, or electoral reasons, policymakers should recognize that symbolism matters in politics. Elections are national events meant to unite citizens around a shared democratic purpose. When an election coincides with a date associated with historical mourning for a significant section of the country, there is a risk that the symbolism overshadows the democratic exercise itself. nigeria.description: By Demola Akinyemi ILORIN – The Federal Government has concluded plans to establish an office of the National Sports Commission (NSC) in Kwara State, following the development of sports facilities by the administration of Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq. He said the officials expressed satisfaction with the facilities at the state stadium complex and indicated that the proposed NSC office would be established in the state. According to him, the development reflects the growing recognition of Kwara’s investment in sports infrastructure. Magaji said the state’s stadium complex could boast of some of the best squash court facilities in the world, adding that Kwara contingents to national and international sporting competitions had recorded improved medal-winning performances. He attributed the development to investments in sports infrastructure and efforts to promote sporting activities in the state. Also speaking, the Special Adviser and Counsellor to the Governor, Alhaji Saad Salahudeen, said AbdulRazaq’s contributions to governance, politics, youth development and national development would continue to attract attention in the years ahead. business.description: Bitcoin Magazine U.S. Treasury Cuts Off MEXC From U.S. Financial System Over Alleged $16 Billion in Illicit Flows The U.S. Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order Friday that will cut offshore exchange MEXC Global off from the American banking system over alleged links to sanctions evasion by Iran, North Korea and Russia, the department said . FinCEN’s order, published as a PDF pending Federal Register placement, finds MEXC a “primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance” under section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. Thirty days after that Register notice, covered U.S. financial institutions will be barred from any funds transfer — including convertible virtual currency — to or from MEXC. Reuters reported the same cut-off Friday afternoon. Treasury framed the move as part of Operation Economic Outcast. It is not an OFAC sanctions designation: the order says it does not rewrite Bank Secrecy Act duties or OFAC rules, and it is a FinCEN funds-transmittal ban rather than a Section 311 proposed rulemaking. Treasury alleges MEXC facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit flows from May 2021 through May 2026, including nearly $1.5 billion tied to Russian sanctions evasion and about $22 million linked to Iran’s Central Bank and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Qods Force. The platform was still processing trades with sanctioned Garantex and successor Grinex as recently as June 2026, more than four years after OFAC designated Garantex, the release says. What the order does — and when The order , signed by FinCEN Deputy Director Jimmy L. Kirby, covers MEXC Global and named affiliates operating outside the United States, including Seychelles-incorporated MEXC Global Ltd / MX Global Ltd, Estonia’s MEXC Estonia OÜ, Switzerland’s GIDA Technology AG and the U.K.’s MXC Global Ltd, plus successors. Covered institutions face civil or criminal penalties for willful violations. Until the Federal Register publishes the notice, the 30-day clock has not started. As of Friday evening eastern time the Register’s public index still showed no MEXC document, matching the order’s own cover note that publication is pending. Background on MEXC Founded in 2018 and formerly branded MXC, MEXC ranks among the world’s 20 largest centralized crypto venues by volume. Treasury puts daily turnover above $1 billion and reserves near $5 billion as of mid-2026, with access claimed across more than 170 countries. The exchange already lists the United States as a prohibited jurisdiction in its user terms, so Friday’s action mainly hits any remaining dollar rails, banking partners and counterparties that still touch U.S. institutions. entertainment.title: From the Sky to the Earth To You: Earth & Sky by Banke Kuku
entertainment.description: With Earth & Sky , her Spring/Summer 2027 collection, Banke Kuku turns to nature’s most essential cycle: the sky gives rain, the rain feeds the earth, and the earth gives back. Reimagining the water cycle as a circle of life, the collection celebrates the abundance that flows from it. Earth & Sky is built around seven prints in three families. The Sky family is led by the hero print, Bougainvillea Sky, with watercolour bougainvillea, bees, butterflies and birds drifting across a turquoise ground, alongside Dove Sky and Daybreak Sky. The Earth family, Yellow Trumpet and Flower Bud, draws on flowering plants such as Costus spectabilis . The Rain family pairs Raindrop, a glossy, near-photographic print set against the softness of the watercolours, with the Kuku Monogram in fresh colourways. Sky prints are finished with hand-embroidered clouds and raindrops on flowing kaftans and kimono robes. Speaking on the inspiration, Creative Director Banke Kuku shares: “I never start with a sketch. I start with a feeling, and for Earth & Sky, that feeling was abundance. This year I became a mother for the first time, and everywhere I looked, nature was reflecting that same fullness back at me. This is my most personal collection.” A CYCLE OF GIVING BACK In nature, nothing is wasted, and everything returns. Earth & Sky carries that principle as its message: what we take from the earth, we must give back. That principle extends into how Banke Kuku approaches production. The brand maintains a no-waste policy, finding uses for offcuts rather than discarding them, while its seasonless approach allows pieces to remain part of the collection beyond a single season. Banke Kuku also uses digital printing, which consumes less heat and water than conventional printing methods, and continues to reduce its use of man-made fabrics in favour of more conscious material choices. Its commitment to the natural world extends beyond its collections, including its work with the Nigerian Conservation Foundation and its Re-Green Movement, which supports afforestation and the restoration of Nigeria’s natural environment. For its latest limited edition, Maison Martell has brought together Nigerian music superstar Davido and Ghanaian visual artist Prince Gyasi to create a new expression of its prestigious XO cognac , inspired by the sound, movement and global influence of Afrobeats. The Martell Afrobeats Limited Edition XO will be unveiled in Nigeria on November 6, following the collection’s global launch in New York on October 28. At the heart of the collaboration is Prince Gyasi’s distinctive artistic language. Known for his vibrant colours and imaginative compositions, Gyasi has created an original artwork of Davido that features on the limited-edition bottle and presentation box. The design draws inspiration from the landscapes of West Africa, bringing together Martell’s iconic blue with shades of amber and gold. The blue reflects the rhythmic flow of the ocean, while the golden tones evoke sunlit sands and the warmth of African sunsets. entertainment.title: Adaugo Nwankpa: What a Career Transition Taught Me About Starting Over
entertainment.description: One year and two months ago, I took a career pivot. I moved from being a digital media professional writing stories, articles and shaping narratives to becoming an analyst in the energy sector, working across the oil and gas and renewable subsectors. The journey across these two industries that are worlds apart has taught me lessons on starting over You are never really starting from scratch No matter what you are starting over at or what you are getting into, it is important to realise that you are never truly starting from zero. Where ‘zero’ means the state of having nothing: skills, experience, network, intelligence, and others. While it may indeed appear that you do not have the things you consider as being critical to starting over, you actually have what you have: the knowledge, skills and experiences that have shaped your life and marked your journey up to this present moment, and this is invaluable. Also, having a strong knowledge of yourself is also an incredible resource when starting over, as it helps you to discern and differentiate challenges that are due to your personality, and challenges that are due to the circumstance of starting over. Your ‘Next Best Move’ is hidden within your network When we think of network, it is easy to limit it to close friends, relatives or even acquaintances. This is quite a restrictive and limiting view of the concept of network. Your network also includes ‘strangers’ and your internet community. In my case, I knew of the opportunity in the energy sector through a friend whom I had met on Instagram. It gets more interesting. By the time I was preparing for my first interview, I knew that I had zero knowledge about the current state of the sector. Thanks again to Instagram, I reached out to someone I followed who I knew worked in the sector, and she offered a free virtual coffee chat. I went into the interview more confident in what value I could offer and what mattered for such a role. Transferable skills are invaluable Prior to my career pivot, my only exposure to the energy sector aside from buying fuel and gas was a seminar paper I had written in my final year investigating annual shifts in fuel pump prices. However, I audited my skills and qualifications and noted that I also had highly transferable skills. I had communication, business development and a good knowledge and expertise in using Canva. For you, it could be international exposure, multiple languages or something else you think is insignificant. No matter what you are starting over at, you have something that can be transferred from where you were to where you are or where you want to be. Adopt a growth mindset In today’s world, flexibility, adaptability and agility are your currencies for greatness. entertainment.title: Loving Itohan: Come for the Love Story, Stay for Everything Loving Itohan Says About Grief and Family
entertainment.description: Nancy Isime ‘s first film as executive producer, from GREOH Studios, is a beautifully shot story about the love that holds a family together when life falls apart. Some films you watch. Others stay with you. Loving Itohan is the second kind. It opens like the love story you think you already know: a radiant bride, an Edo wedding, coral beads and gold everywhere. You settle in for romance. Then, slowly, the film shows you its heart, and it is so much bigger than a love story. At its centre is Itohan, played by Nancy Isime, a woman whose world is shaken by loss and by truths she never saw coming. What follows is a story about grief, the quiet kind that stays in a home long after the visitors have gone. It is about family, the people who hold us up and sometimes weigh us down. And it is about love that has to keep choosing to stay, even when it hurts. You will see yourself in it. In the person trying to hold everyone together. In the things left unsaid at the dinner table. In the slow, uneven way healing actually happens. A film that looks as good as it feels The cinematography deserves its own round of applause. Every frame feels deliberate, from the rich reds and golds of Edo tradition to the close, quiet moments where a single look says everything. The camera knows when to celebrate and when to simply sit with a character in her pain. This is a film made for the big screen. There is a reason it all feels so assured. Loving Itohan is from GREOH Studios , and Jade studio has never been afraid to go big, with daring, genre-bending stories like Gangs of Lagos. This time, GREOH goes deep instead, trading spectacle for the messy, tender feelings we all carry. True to form, it also hands the director’s chair to a fresh talent, Orobosa Ikponmwen , the latest in a line of new directors the studio has backed, from Kayode Kasum to Loukman Ali. And for Nancy Isime, this is her very first project as an executive producer. You can feel how much of herself she has poured into it, in front of the camera and behind it. Alongside her, Uzor Arukwe, Martha Ehinome Orhiere, Dorathy Bachor, Grace Dein Coker, Chioma Nwosu, Florence Sunday and newcomer Obehi Aburime bring the family to life. Don’t judge it by the trailer If the trailer has you thinking you know where this is going, trust us, you don’t. Go with someone you love. Bring tissues. And maybe call your mum afterwards. entertainment.title: Dayo Akinbode: What Travelling to Cuba Taught Me About Money
entertainment.description: I went to Cuba for the salsa, the cigars, the rum and those gorgeous vintage cars. I never imagined that, somewhere between admiring the colourful streets and enjoying the Caribbean sunshine, I would receive an unexpected lesson in money management. Looking back, I can laugh about my experience. But at the time, discovering how much I might have been overpaying left me wondering how much my ignorance had already cost me. Cuba had a way of making me feel as though I had stepped into a film. Imagine standing in a sun-drenched plaza, a Cuban cigar in your hand, the warm Caribbean breeze brushing against your skin, and music floating through the air. Around you, buildings painted in faded yellows, dusty pinks and weathered blues stand proudly, their grand colonial facades and ornate balconies carrying stories from another century. Then comes the rumble of an engine. You turn to see a cherry-red vintage car gliding past, followed by a bubblegum-pink beauty that seems to have driven straight out of the 1950s. Everywhere you look, vibrant colours, rich history and lively movement bring the streets to life And the cars! Oh, the cars! Later, I would find myself riding in a neon-green convertible along the coast, the wind whipping through my hair as the blue Caribbean Sea stretched beside me. I felt wonderfully alive. Cuba was giving me everything I had hoped for: beauty, music, history and the thrill of discovering somewhere different. I was so captivated by everything that I paid little attention to the money in my purse. I visited Cuba in 2019, when the country had two official currencies: the Cuban convertible peso, known as the CUC, and the Cuban peso, known as the CUP. To an unsuspecting tourist like me, this arrangement was a recipe for confusion. I was carrying CUC notes, commonly used by visitors because that is what the banks give you in exchange for your USD notes. The CUC notes looked different from the CUP notes I would later encounter. CUC notes featured monuments, while CUP notes carried the faces of Cuban national heroes, including José Martí and Camilo Cienfuegos. But at the time, I barely noticed the distinction. Money was money, or so I thought. Whenever I needed to pay for something, I reached into my purse, brought out my CUC notes and settled the bill. I was enjoying my holiday and had no reason to suspect my wallet was quietly making it more expensive than necessary. Then, one time, I was given change in a currency different from the familiar CUC. I looked at the notes in my hand and immediately felt that something was wrong. These were not the notes I was accustomed to using. I did not recognise them, and I was not about to walk away with money I did not understand. So, I rejected the change. Imagine my surprise when the cashier and another customer explained to me that the notes were perfectly valid Cuban money! That was when I got my crash course in Cuban economics. sports.description: UCF threw away a three-score, second-half lead on the road for the second time in just over a month. Only this time, Alonza Barnett III — the redshirt senior brought in from James Madison to lead the Knights back to prominence — delivered a signature, final-minute drive for the win. Barnett hit tight end Caden Piening for a 6-yard touchdown pass with one second remaining, and Will Stone knocked through the decisive PAT in a 33-32 rally past Kansas on Nov. 7 at David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium. The Knights improved to 5-4 overall and 3-3 in the Big 12, moving to within one win of bowl eligibility with three games left. More importantly, Scott Frost and his players finally silenced the conversation of UCF's woes on the road. The 12-game skid, dating back to September 2024, is dead. Asked if he could describe his emotions after watching the Knights surrender a 26-7 lead and complete a final comeback, Frost said, "I could try to describe it, but it would come up short." "We've been involved in two pretty special games, as good of college football games as I've been involved (with) in a long time," Frost added, referring to UCF's double-overtime win over BYU on Oct. 24. "I thought it was two evenly matched teams and just the way the game went was really strange to me. I feel blessed that we were able to go down and get the play at the end of the game." sports.title: One daring shot was all La Salle needed to repeat as state soccer champs
sports.description: PROVIDENCE – Camryn Bromage just couldn't help herself, and that turned out to be the best thing for La Salle on this Saturday afternoon at Rhode Island College. The junior midfielder had time to take a shot midway through the first half against Cumberland. That it was from all of 35 yards, or that coach Stephanie Goulet would have preferred a pass elsewhere, will ultimately just become details in a story they'll remember for years to come. Bromage managed to find the net and make the difference at Alumni Stadium as the Rams sealed back-to-back Division I titles with a 1-0 win over the Clippers under gray skies on Nov. 7. "My coach was like, 'Do not take that shot.' It was a little far out," Bromage said. "But I had the space, I had the opportunity and I just shot it." Watch RI high school sports on NFHS! Bromage took aim in the 15th minute after a tense start between a pair of familiar contenders. Her right-footed effort skipped at the top of the 6-yard box and found its way inside the right post, aided by turf still slick from the overnight rain. That moment allowed La Salle to flip what was its lone defeat of the season, a loss by the same score line against Cumberland at home. "It's a wet game," Bromage said. "The field is slippery. It just so happened it went through." The Rams kept a 12th clean sheet of the season to bring this one home, with central defender Jill Handrahan claiming tournament Most Valuable Player honors. Grace Keenan was forced to make just two saves, and one of those came off a corner kick when Shea Maher tried to force one home with her chest in the 54th minute. "I know a lot of the girls on their team," Handrahan said. "I know how good they are. Going into it I was a little nervous." The Clippers nearly opened the scoring in the first minute. Paynter Maher's cross off the right wing flashed across an open net, but Milana Izzo couldn't get a touch on it to put it away. Cumberland didn't force a save from Keenan before the break, with La Salle gradually taking control of the play as the half progressed. "I feel like we brought the energy," Handrahan said. "Everybody was just working so hard." The Rams (14-1-3) and Clippers (15-2-2) exploded for a combined 12 goals while dispatching North Kingstown and Mt. Hope, respectively, in the semifinals. This was a different sort of 80 minutes in the title round, and La Salle joined the Skippers among programs to finish off recent repeat titles at the top level. North Kingstown beat the Rams in 2021 and 2022 before La Salle returned the favor in 2025. "It's hard to win it two times in a row," Bromage said. "I'm just so happy we were able to accomplish that for our seniors and for everybody." CUMBERLAND (0): No scoring. LA SALLE (1): Camryn Bromage; assist – Lila Slagle. Halftime – LS, 1-0. sports.description: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images Norfolk State’s Michael Vick gives explanation for failed victory formation in 29-28 loss appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . It looked like Michael Vick and his Norfolk State Spartans were closing in on a huge in-conference win against a surging North Carolina Central Eagles team , but the unthinkable happened with 1:34 left. North Carolina Central had no timeouts, and Norfolk State had the ball and could have run out the clock to secure the victory. But instead, the Spartans ran another play and ultimately fumbled, leading North Carolina Central to recover and ultimately score a touchdown to surge ahead 29-28. Michael Vick on the crucial fumble that opened the door for Norfolk State's stunning defeat to North Carolina Central. @WTKR3 pic.twitter.com/rJBWUCF9Dx — Marc Davis (@marcdavissports) November 7, 2026 Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) In postgame comments, Vick tried to explain what happened. “I don’t know what happened at the end of the game. I put my headset down, I called victory formation. All we had to do was just take a knee and nail the clock out. That’s just situational football. I don’t know what happened in regards to that. I looked up and we was running the ball, and then I seen the fumble. But my final instructions was victory formation. That’s when you kneel it out, and they had, I think, zero timeouts left, and the game was over practically.” When a reporter asked him to clarify, Vick repeated that he called victory and said he doesn’t know why a run play was called. “I put my headset down, and I took my headset off ’cause all we had to do was just run it three times, or two times, or kneel it out. I just called victory. I don’t know what happened. A run play was called. I looked up, I seen us running the ball. I don’t know what happened. I really don’t. I don’t know what the play call was. I don’t know why we even ran that play.” Vick said the play will be used as a teaching example across the country and stressed once more that he called victory formation. “People will look at that and that’ll go on as a teaching tape for a lot of teams across the country for years to come. sports.title: Elmira, Horseheads fall in NYSPHSAA girls soccer regional finals
sports.description: A pair of Section 4 girls soccer champions from Chemung County saw their seasons come to a close Saturday, Nov. 7 at Chenango Valley High School. Elmira lost by a 1-0 score to Section 1's Arlington in a New York State Public High School Athletic Association Class AAA regional final/state quarterfinal. Horseheads came up short, 3-1, against Section 11's Northport in a Class AA regional final that followed. The lone Section 4 girls team to advance to the state final four was Greene, which edged Tully, 2-1, in overtime in a Class C quarterfinal Saturday behind two goals from Miah Cragle. Maine-Endwell lost to Section 5's Pittsford, 5-0, in Class A. Margaretville fell to Section 10's Lisbon Central, 3-1, in Class D. Class AAA: Arlington 1, Elmira 0 Chase Harris scored the game's only goal with 29 minutes, 58 seconds remaining and the Admirals held off the Express. A strong effort from goalie Delaney Billbe helped keep Elmira within striking distance. Express head coach Zach Sarno praised her play and that of the defense, which he said was "stellar" all season. Arlington (14-1-5) is ranked third in Class AAA by the New York State Sports Writers Association. Elmira is ranked 24th. Elmira finished with an 11-6 record that included a 2-1 victory over Ithaca in the Section 4 championship game . The Express' roster is predominantly underclassmen. "You know it's always going to be a battle when you get to this level, especially when you're playing some teams that you're not familiar with," Sarno said. "I think we worked extremely hard. We left it all out here and that's all you can ask for. ... I'm just proud of the girls today. "We work hard, but we're still a growing team. Very, very young and I would say we did everything we could this year. We're going to continue to get better." Arlington will face fellow Section 1 team Albertus Magnus in a state semifinal at 10 a.m. Saturday, Nov. 14 at Dryden High School. More: Matchups and scores for the 2026 Section 4 girls soccer tournaments Class AA: Northport 3, Horseheads 1 Maddie Ribble scored the game's final goal for Horseheads with 14 minutes remaining as the Blue Raiders' season came to a close after capturing a third consecutive Section 4 title . Ava DeMarco and Caitlin Cocks scored first-half goals for the Admirals. DeMarco scored her second goal seven minutes into the second half. Northport (16-2) will play fellow Section 11 team West Islip in a state semifinal at 2:30 p.m. Nov. 14 at Dryden High School. Northport is ranked third in the state in Class AA. Horseheads finished with a 10-4-2 record. The Blue Raiders are ranked 20th in New York in Class AA. sports.title: Bexley edges Fairfield Union in regional soccer championship game
sports.description: HEATH — The Fairfield Union girls’ soccer team started their Division III regional championship with a bang when senior Maddi Mitchell scored a goal on an assist from Makayla Rawlins in the first minute of the game against Bexley to give the Falcons a quick lead. However, it didn’t last, as the Lions were able to counter with a pair of goals and held on for a hard-fought 2-1 victory to end the Falcons’ season on Saturday, Nov. 7, at Heath High School. More: Fairfield Union girls soccer wins regional semifinal vs Tri-Valley Fairfield Union was making only its second-ever appearance in an Elite Eight game. Ironically, the Falcons’ only other appearance came five years ago against Bexley, and they lost that game, 2-1. Kaeda Miller finished with 11 saves in goal for the Falcons on Saturday. It was a tough way to end the season, but Fairfield Union has nothing to be ashamed of. The Falcons finish with a 15-5-2 record, placing second (5-1) in the Mid-State League-Buckeye Division. The Falcons reached the regional final by beating Hillsboro 8-0 and Sheridan 3-1, before upsetting top-ranked Marietta 1-0 in the Southeast district championship. It marked the fourth time in the last four years that the Falcons have won a district title. From there, Fairfield Union defeated Tri-Valley 2-0 in the regional semifinal at Logan. Senior Kyla Gasser finished her outstanding career with several records. She scored her 78 th career goal in the win against Tri-Valley, which ties the school record held by Taylor Davis. Gasser also has school records for most assists in a season with 30 and most career assists with 60. Fairfield Union coach Casey Bischof also won his 200 th career win earlier this season. sports.title: “Embarrassing”: Cowboys Legend Calls Out Brian Schottenheimer & Co. Amid Disappointing 3–5 Start
sports.description: Dec 25, 2025: Dallas Cowboys Head Coach Brian Schottenheimer during the Washington Commanders game against the Dallas Cowboys at Northwest Stadium in Landover, MD. /CSM Landover United States of America – ZUMAc04_ 20251225_zma_c04_018 Copyright: xJustinxCooperx ©IMAGO/ZUMA Press Wire The Cowboys are 3-5 after a 33-30 overtime loss to the Arizona Cardinals , a game they led 14-0 before the Cardinals rallied. Jerry Jones has ruled out a midseason coaching change, but Brian Schottenheimer is 10-14-1 since taking over, and a franchise legend has now publicly questioned the direction of the team. “Let’s say this, it was the Cowboys, and I’ve said it in different phases that you have to go through the coaching staff preparation, come to the sideline to adapt what’s going on,” James Washington said on the Cowboys Country Football . “Let’s focus just on coaching staff time management. Embarrassing because the coaching staff don’t got this thing under control. Offense, defense, and I’ve always kept it simple on defense. Containment. Every long run, there was no one to turn the ball back inside.” It’s harsh, but Sunday gave him plenty to work with. Dallas, now sitting at three wins and five losses, handed away a 14-point fourth-quarter lead to Arizona. For a while, the Cowboys looked comfortable. They forced two turnovers, piled up five sacks, and held the Cardinals to three first-half points. Jacoby Brissett was struggling, and then Gardner Minshew replaced him. That’s when the defense came apart. Arizona scored touchdowns on four straight possessions to finish regulation, tie the game, and push it to overtime. The Cardinals put up 27 points in the second half, outgained Dallas 286 to 157, converted four of five third downs, and went three for three in the red zone. The total yardage was 467 to 261. This came right after Philadelphia ran for 121 yards on them. A Cowboys icon isn't holding back on Dallas' coaching staff. Subscribe to stay on top of the drama unfolding in America's Team. The defense is the biggest concern. Dallas allows 385.4 yards a game, the worst mark in the league. Michael Irvin has never been shy about the Cowboys, but this week he went further than most. “That’s an easy bet, Stephen A. Like, you think that’s something big,” Irvin said. “Anybody would bet their check on it, because anybody can do better. Anybody. There is no worse that you can be than they are right now.” He kept going. “There is no such thing as lower than this, or worse than this, or not as good as this. They are the worst. So anybody, anybody, my dead mom can coach them better,” Irvin continued. Schottenheimer’s own words haven’t helped. After a 13-point showing at Green Bay, he called himself an “elite playcaller in this league.” The Arizona game made that hard to defend. The offense has also lost some of what made it interesting. Last season, extra pre-snap motion was one of the biggest changes under Schottenheimer, giving the unit a way to create better matchups.

science.title: NASA Awards Moon Base Transportation, Technology, Science Projects
science.description: Artist’s concept of living and working at Moon Base. Credit: NASA NASA announced a suite of awards and mission updates on Saturday to expand the agency’s Moon Base exploration, science, and infrastructure capabilities. The investments will advance commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover named PROMISE, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure as the agency works with American industry to establish a sustained presence on the Moon’s South Pole. The agency shared the news at the MAX POWER aerospace expo and air show at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. “We are building the Moon Base mission by mission,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Today’s announcements expand nearly every part of that campaign, using the playbook that carried NASA through its greatest eras: fly often, learn, apply those lessons, and get more better and more capable with every mission. When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface.” “In the eight months since Ignition, we’ve made incredible strides in accomplishing the near impossible: establishing a permanent outpost on the lunar surface,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. “We’ve consolidated numerous efforts into a streamlined program, evolving our human exploration architecture into an iterative and sustained campaign for Moon Base technology development and implementation. Most importantly, we’ve taken action, awarding new contracts and forging new partnerships to accelerate development.” Moon Base cargo landers To strengthen the cargo lander network needed to support the Moon Base, NASA selected eight companies for the next phase of its CLPS ( Commercial Lunar Payload Services ) initiative. The companies are eligible to compete for future lunar surface delivery missions under the new CLPS 2 contract: Blue Origin Firefly Aerospace Intuitive Machines iSpace US Lockheed Martin Space Northrop Grumman Space Systems SpaceX Voyager Technologies Under the CLPS 2 framework, the companies will provide lunar delivery services, including managing, building, and operating landers that transport NASA science, technology, and infrastructure payloads to the Moon. The CLPS 2 framework is a 10-year, multiple-award, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity master contract with a combined maximum value of $10 billion. NASA increased the value of the current CLPS 1.0 contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support initial Phase One Moon Base objectives. The original CLPS contract will remain in place through November 2028, with an additional five-year period to complete awarded lunar deliveries through November 2033. Nuclear-powered Moon rover NASA also announced it is moving forward with development of PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration) . Carrying science instruments and technology demonstrations, the six-wheeled rover will land at the Moon

science.title: NASA Seeks Next Generation of Explorers to Join Astronaut Corps
science.description: NASA announced its 2025 Astronaut Candidate Class on Sept. 22, 2025, at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Credit: NASA/Helen Arase Vargas NASA is looking for the explorers who will help write the next chapter of human spaceflight. Applications are now open for the agency’s next class of astronauts, who will join NASA as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base, and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars. The next generation of astronauts will train to operate on the lunar surface, live and work beyond Earth, and take on missions that will push the boundaries of human exploration farther than ever before. U.S. citizens interested in joining the astronaut corps have until 11:59 p.m. EST Thursday, Dec. 3, to submit their completed application materials at: https://go.nasa.gov/3WyvlQi “This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “The people we select could walk on the Moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars. Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage. NASA’s astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 7, 1992: NASA launches Mars Global Surveyor, its 1st Mars mission in 20 years at the time, to map the Red Planet like never before
science.description: null On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years! The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner , Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water. Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites. Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected. But a space maneuver accidentally exposed one of its batteries to the sun, and the spacecraft lost power. It fell silent forever in November 2006 . NASA launches the Mars Global Surveyor to Mars on a Delta II rocket on Nov. 7, 1996. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered As the first successful Mars mission since the two Viking launches in 1975, Mars Global Surveyor ushered in a new era of exploration of the Red Planet, not only through its own contributions to orbit-based science, but by serving a relay for surface-based rovers. As such, it became a primary pipeline for multiple concurrent Mars missions. "The [Mars Global Surveyor] mission overhauled scientists' understanding of Mars by studying the entire Martian surface, atmosphere and interior. Major findings included dramatic evidence that water still flows on Mars in short bursts down hillside gullies, and the identification of water-related mineral deposits leading to selection of a Mars rover landing site for a subsequent mission," read a NASA description of the probe. Mars Global Surveyor sent back more than 240,000 images to Earth during its nine active years. Want more space history? science.title: Send your name to Saturn's moon Titan with NASA's upcoming Dragonfly mission
science.description: null We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission. Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. 15, 2027. The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034. "Nearly a billion miles away, an extraordinary destination awaits. Titan has an atmosphere, rivers and lakes, seasons, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material," NASA officials wrote in the event page. "Upon arrival in 2034, Dragonfly will fly from place to place on this intriguing world to uncover clues about this remarkable moon, and the chemistry that could help us understand the ingredients for life." Dragonfly will be one of just a few flying crafts on another world, with the first being NASA's plucky Ingenuity mini-helicopter that arrived on Mars along with the still-running Perseverance rover in 2021. Ingenuity was only designed to make five flights, but made it to 72 until its blades were damaged during a landing on Jan. 18, 2024. NASA is now planning a SkyFall mission on Mars that would use three helicopters, and which may launch as soon as late 2028 for the Red Planet. Dragonfly, however, is not the first mission to Titan: that would be Huygens , which operated for just a few hours on Jan. 14, 2005 after deploying from the Cassini spacecraft. Huygens was the first lander on an outer solar system world, and measured Titan's atmosphere and took data from the surface. A mosaic image of Saturn's moon Titan composed of images produced by the Cassini spacecraft. (Image credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona/University of Idaho) For its part, Cassini flew by Titan more than 100 times before the mission concluded in September 2017 , providing valuable long-term data about the moon from above. Dragonfly aims to show the moon from up close for about 3.3 Earth years. Its destinations will include dunes and a young impact crater called Selk, according to NASA. "Dragonfly is expected to make one flight every one to two Titan days, which is called a Tsol and lasts about 16 Earth days," NASA officials added of the mission . Dragonfly will stop at a variety of geologic sites, where it will collect samples of surface material for analysis inside the rotorcraft by a suite of scientific instruments." With LucasArts' successor calling the shots and coordinating a multitude of projects set in a galaxy far, far away, even EA's latest efforts like Squadrons and the Jedi series have taken bigger and bolder swings. Now, in 2026, the full potential of the Star Wars universe has become clearer with specific releases squarely aimed at niche audiences. It's become clear that future Star Wars games needn't be expensive endeavors full of familiar faces or concepts. Starlink is SpaceX's LEO broadband megaconstellation, which consists of more than 11,000 active satellites. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
science.description: null On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it. The Tycho supernova remnant as seen by the Chandra X-ray space telescope. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/RIKEN & GSFC/T. Sato et al; Optical: DSS) Why it mattered The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572 , is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star. While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky. "The 16th century exploding star, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia , was seen in daylight for about two weeks, and remained visible to the naked eye for 16 months," the University of California Berkeley wrote in 2004 . "Brahe's meticulous record of the brightening and dimming of the supernova now allows astronomers to identify its 'light signature" as that of a Type Ia supernova." "This was at the end of the Dark Ages in Europe, and these observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable," astronomer Alex Filippenko, who led a 2004 study on the origins of the Tycho supernova, said at the time . Today, astronomers are closely watching another star that might explode. Called T Corona Borealis , or the Blaze Star , the object is expected to be on the verge of exploding in a nova (a star explosion that is smaller than a supernova and may not destroy the star). is one of 11 known stars observed to have recurring nova explosions within gaps of 100 years or so. science.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
science.description: null Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!" The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky. And the view is only going to get better in the days and weeks to come! Ascending in the morning In terms of morning visibility, Venus is now in a literal and figurative sense "rising to the occasion." It's now rising before the break of dawn, more than 90 minutes before sunrise. From here on, it will rise three minutes earlier each day, so that by Dec. 17 it will rise 3 hours and 50 minutes before sunrise and blaze in a completely dark sky for more than two hours before the first vestige of morning twilight. It will reach peak brilliance on Nov. 29, when it will shine at an eye-popping magnitude of -4.9. That's 12 times brighter than its nearest planetary competitor, Jupiter and a full 25 times more dazzling than Sirius, the brightest of all stars. If you live in a rural location with no light pollution to interfere, you might be able to make out that it is casting a visible shadow and if you follow it right on through sunrise, it will be evident to your naked eye in full daylight: a tiny white speck plainly evident against the blue daytime sky. In a way, we could even regard Venus as this year's version of a "Christmas Star," glowing with stunning radiance ". . . in the east" like the biblical quote mentioned in St. Matthew. What goes up, must come down After reaching its high point in terms of morning visibility in mid-December, Venus will start a long, slow slide back toward the sun, rising about 1½ minutes later each morning from New Year's Day through late March. By then, Venus will be coming up as dawn is breaking, roughly 100 minutes before sunrise. Venus will continue to get gradually lower and rise progressively later during the spring and by late June it will be coming up less than an hour before sunrise, ultimately vanishing into the bright dawn twilight by July. Venus will then go on a "summer sabbatical" of sorts and will not reappear again until about this time next year when it will begin a very fine evening apparition. So, if any of your friends or relatives remark to you that they saw a "strange UFO" on the way to work or school recently, you now can set them straight. It's not E.T. It's only Venus. science.title: Record-breaking, fast-spinning magnet could help uncover new physics
science.description: Magnets can be made to levitate by the Meissner effect Science History Images / Alamy A tiny magnet that levitates within a superconductor trap may be the fastest spinning object visible to the naked eye, and one of the fastest spinning objects ever made. In the future, it could be used in experiments searching for mysterious dark matter particles and aid the development of quantum technologies. Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity with perfect efficiency, and they also expel any magnetic field that tries to permeate them – a phenomenon known as the Meissner effect. Because of this, a magnet placed above a superconductor experiences repulsive magnetic forces and starts to levitate. Tao Wang at the Agency for Science Technology and Research in Singapore and his colleagues have now set one such levitating magnet spinning at an unprecedently fast rate. Read more A miniature magnet rivals behemoths in strength for the first time The researchers used a spherical magnet made from neodymium, iron and boron that was about 30 micrometres wide, similar to the width of a fine human hair. They placed it in a cylindrical container made from lead, then enclosed that container in a chamber devoid of air, or a vacuum chamber. Advertisement Next, they used liquid helium to cool the whole setup to approximately -269°C (-452°F), only a few degrees above the coldest possible temperature . Under these extreme circumstances, lead behaved as a superconductor and the lack of air meant that the magnet could levitate within it without bumping into any particles. The team set the magnet spinning with a magnetic coil, ultimately pushing this tiny rotor to 138 million revolutions per minute. Wang says the magnet’s spinning was also very stable: it would take 17 days for its spinning speed to decrease by 50 per cent, something that would typically happen more quickly due to interactions between the magnet and its environment. “In terms of how many turns it makes before slowing down significantly, this is in the same league as the Earth’s spinning,” he says. “This, so far, is the fastest magnetically levitated rotor.” The record for the fastest rotating human-made object is also held by a levitated sphere, but that one was nano-sized, so invisible to the naked eye, and levitated by laser beams. science.title: An unexpected feedback loop may be driving mega heatwaves
science.description: Land scorched by a fire in Wennington, London, during the record-breaking heatwave in 2022 Shutterstock Mid-latitude regions such as Europe are set to suffer more intense heatwaves than previously thought, according to new research that has uncovered a three-way feedback loop that amplifies extreme heat conditions. Heatwaves across the world have shocked scientists with their scale and severity in recent years, with heat extremes dramatically outstripping both historical records and the predictions of climate models. Read more Extreme heat is now making cities unlivable. How can we survive it? In the UK in 2022, temperatures exceeded 40°C (104 ° F) for the first time in history, despite predictions that such a milestone was probably still years away. Likewise, the 2021 heatwave in the Pacific Northwest saw temperatures hit extremes that far outstripped climate model projections. Advertisement Researchers have been scrambling to understand why very extreme heat is occurring more frequently, and with greater intensity, than expected at this level of warming. One team thinks the answer lies partly in the soil. Scientists already knew that high-pressure systems allow more solar radiation to reach Earth’s surface, heating up the land. They also knew that higher temperatures dry soils more quickly, removing the cooling effect provided by evaporation, thereby further amplifying heatwaves. Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter Now it seems that when temperatures climb high enough, dry soil, high pressure and extreme heat can amplify each other further, with dry soil helping to sustain high-pressure systems in the atmosphere. “Basically, the soils that are affected by circulation pattern also start to affect back on the circulation pattern itself,” says Kai Kornhuber at the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Austria. This three-way feedback effect makes extreme heatwaves 10 per cent hotter than they would otherwise be, according to the research by Kornhuber and his colleagues – a factor not fully accounted for in climate model projections. This will have serious consequences for our ability to cope with future extreme heat. “Ten per cent hotter or colder can really make a difference between a heatwave and a record-shattering heatwave,” says Kornhuber. “We’re facing so many critical thresholds in social and biophysical systems that an extra 10 per cent can really lead to temperatures that are then quite damaging.” Read more Is a broken jet stream causing extreme weather that lasts longer? This may include serious public health consequences, a breakdown of vital infrastructure such as transport links and energy grids, crop failures and the collapse of ecosystems. science.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
science.description: null The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece. That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target. What's happening and when to look The Andromeda galaxy is at its most dramatic in photographs, not an eyepiece. (Image credit: Created using Canva and a base image from Starry Night) Early November is an excellent time to find M31 from the Northern Hemisphere. It's high and well placed during the evening, and this week the moon is becoming particularly cooperative. New Moon falls around Nov. 9, giving us several evenings with little or no moonlight to wash out faint deep-sky objects. I usually begin with the star Alpheratz, one of the corner stars of the Great Square of Pegasus. You go two stars left, two stars up, and you arrive at M31. Another route — and a good way to check you're in the right place — starts in Cassiopeia, the distinctive W-shaped constellation high in the northeastern sky on autumn evenings. You can use its second V-shape as an arrow pointing straight at M31. You can do that star-hop with the naked eye or a pair of binoculars, but M31 is visible to the naked eye only under a very dark sky. However, don't look for a miniature version of the photographs. Expect a faint, elongated patch with a slightly brighter middle. There's another beginner trap to avoid. Images make Andromeda look compact, but its full apparent extent is enormous — several times the width of the full moon — and our eyes usually pick up only the much brighter central region. science.title: Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight
science.description: null Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world. The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. Even using a tool called a coronagraph to block the star isn't enough to reveal the planet, as that doesn't stop all the starlight. The only solution to this glaring problem is a computer program to wipe out the starlight. "For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference," Jason Wang of Northwestern University explained in a statement . "Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden." There is a problem with this process, however. Even the most stable telescopes "wobble." For instance, the JWST requires cryocoolers to keep its NIRCam instrument super cold, and those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. This movement, however slight, causes a scatter in starlight. The result is enough glare remaining to obscure a planet, but Wang and colleagues developed a new approach to this problem. Telescopes their more stable digital twins The new approach taken by the team is dubbed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), and it involves creating a digital "twin" of a telescope. Essentially a virtual replica that simulates how starlight travels through the telescope's mirrors and reaches its detectors. This twin is then fine-tuned to account for millions of tiny imperfections in the original telescope. The digital twin is then tweaked until it aligns with observations from the actual telescope. Astronomers can then remove the simulated glare from the original image. To assess the validity of the technique, the researchers took a second look at JWST observations of two star systems with known exoplanets, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani , and one system, TYC 5899, with no known planets.
